news.title: Ruby Rippey, former Gavin Newsom staffer, offers new details on their affair 20 years ago
news.text:
SAN FRANCISCO -- A former staffer who had an affair with Gavin Newsom more than 20 years ago offered extensive details in an essay published Tuesday by Vanity Fair, taking issue with how the California governor has more recently characterized what happened.

Newsom, then the mayor of San Francisco, admitted in 2007 that he had an affair in the years prior with Ruby Rippey, his appointments secretary and the wife of his campaign manager, Alex Tourk. Rippey has not spoken much about the scandal as Newsom has risen in politics and emerged as a potential 2028 presidential contender.

In the Vanity Fair piece, Rippey criticizes Newsom's description of the affair and its fallout in a memoir he published earlier this year. He wrote that it was the "briefest of affairs," and recounted how he "came clean" to Tourk, a close friend.

"That detail-subtle but significant-is the one that stays with me," Rippey wrote. "It reads-to me, at least-as a version of events that gives him credit for something I had already done."

Newsom had filed for divorce from his wife, former Fox News host Kimberly Guilfoyle, before the affair, but the relationship with his subordinate was an early political stumbling block for Newsom. Tourk resigned after confronting Newsom about it, and Newsom later held a news conference where he said, "Everything you've read is true and I'm deeply sorry for that."

Still, he was reelected later that year with over 73% of the vote.

"The Governor acknowledged his role and publicly apologized nearly two decades ago when he was still mayor," Newsom spokesperson Izzy Gardon said in a statement to CNN and KGO-TV/ABC7 Eyewitness News in San Francisco, responding to Rippey's essay.

"In the time since, he met his wife, started a family, and has focused on serving Californians. He addressed this chapter of his life, including in his memoir, and out of respect for everyone involved, does not have anything further to add," the statement said.

Newsom's personal life is likely to come under more scrutiny if he runs for president in 2028.

The governor, who has since married Jennifer Siebel Newsom, has been open about his interest in a possible White House bid as he has urged fellow Democrats to stand up more to President Donald Trump and "fight fire with fire."

Writing for Vanity Fair, Rippey traces the start of the affair to the summer of 2005 and said it coincided with a period in her life when she was struggling with alcohol addiction. She said she was accountable for her actions but noted that the #MeToo movement, which started in 2017, opened her eyes to the power imbalance in their relationship.

"Both things are true: I am responsible for what I did. Power does not distribute consequences evenly," Rippey, now sober, wrote. "For my former boss, it is a footnote in a longer arc of ascent. For me, it is the fracture that split my life into before and after."

She said she considered whether to speak out publicly in the aftermath of the affair and was approached about writing a memoir. But she credited Kamala Harris, then the San Francisco district attorney, with giving her the best advice she received.

"I wouldn't say anything right now, Ruby. Just pause. More time will give you better perspective," she said Harris told her.

CNN has reached out to a Harris representative for comment.

news.title: Deadline Passes For Trump To Ask Supreme Court To Reconsider Birthright Citizenship Ruling
news.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The deadline passed Tuesday for the Trump administration to ask the Supreme Court to reconsider its rejection of the president’s birthright citizenship restrictions, with no new filing on the docket.

President Donald Trump vowed to seek a rehearing shortly after the opinion handed him a loss on a signature issue, but by Tuesday the 25-day window had elapsed with no new activity.

A petition would face long odds: The court has not agreed to rehear an argued case in more than 50 years.

The high court’s 6-3 decision in June struck down Trump’s executive order that would have denied automatic citizenship to children born in the United States whose parents are in the U.S. illegally or temporarily.

The Republican president’s restrictions on birthright citizenship had been blocked by several lower courts before reaching the justices, and they did not take effect anywhere in the U.S.

Still, three justices — Samuel Alito, Neil Gorsuch and Clarence Thomas – would have upheld them. A fourth justice, Brett Kavanaugh, found the Constitution wouldn’t block the president’s plan, though he found it did violate a federal law.

A week after the decision came down, Trump said in a social media post he would “be asking for a Rehearing by the United States Supreme Court, IMMEDIATELY.”

The White House and Justice Department did not immediately respond to messages seeking comment.

The last time the Supreme Court granted any petition to change an opinion was in 1965, and the last time it reversed a decision was almost a decade earlier, in a case from 1956, said Aaron-Andrew Bruhl, a law professor at William & Mary Law School.

The bar to grant a petition for rehearing is high. It would require at least one justice who ruled against Trump to change their mind and a majority of the court would have to agree, Bruhl said.

news.title: Senate confirms Jay Clayton as nation's intelligence director
news.text:
WASHINGTON -- The Senate has confirmed Jay Clayton to become head of the nation's intelligence agencies, putting a permanent director in place weeks after President Donald Trump sought to delay his nomination.

Clayton, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York and a former Securities and Exchange Commission chairman, was confirmed 51-47 along party lines. Republicans had initially hoped to confirm Clayton in June, but Trump delayed his hearing in order to allow his temporary pick for the job, Bill Pulte, to take over for several weeks after former director Tulsi Gabbard resigned.

Senators from both parties have expressed concerns about Pulte, a former housing regulator who had no intelligence experience. Pulte was in charge when Trump delivered a speech from the White House earlier this month doubling down on his false claims about the 2020 election, which he lost, and released classified documents that he said were relevant to his arguments.

Democrats have also expressed concerns about Clayton, who lost bipartisan support after a contentious hearing two weeks ago in which he repeatedly refused to say that former President Joe Biden won the 2020 election.

Virginia Sen. Mark Warner, the top Democrat on the Senate Intelligence Committee, said at the end of the hearing that he was "bitterly disappointed" in Clayton after initially praising his nomination.

Warner said he would oppose Clayton's nomination but acknowledged that Democrats are "between a rock and a hard place" with Pulte in the job.

Trump praised Clayton after the vote, writing on social media: "Jay is outstanding in every way, and will do a spectacular job as Director!"

Trump revisits false claims about 2020 election

news.title: Iran Threatens to Block Hormuz Over Use of Frozen Assets
news.text: Tehran: Iran on Tuesday warned that it will block the passage of commercial vessels belonging to companies and countries that use its frozen assets to compensate for damages linked to the recent conflict in West Asia. According to a statement issued by the spokesperson for Iran's Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters and carried by Iranian state media, Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting (IRIB), Iran accused the United States of seeking to use its frozen assets to compensate for vessels damaged during what Tehran described as the "imposed war" against the Islamic Republic. "The US President has announced that in the wake of aggressive actions and continued efforts to destabilise the region," the statement said. Referring to US plans to use Iranian assets, the spokesperson stated that compensation for vessels damaged during the conflict would be drawn from Iran's frozen funds. "The damages to vessels that were damaged during the imposed war against Islamic Iran due to the creation of insecurity by the US military and the violation of the illegal and unsafe route south of the Strait of Hormuz will be paid from Iran's frozen assets," the statement said. The spokesperson warned that if any country or company acted on such plans, Iran's armed forces would prevent their vessels from transiting the Strait of Hormuz. "While warning the criminal US President about the consequences of this illegal action, we announce to all companies and countries that welcome Trump's proposal and use Iran's frozen assets under this title that from now on, the armed forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran will not allow any of their vessels to pass through the Strait of Hormuz," the statement said, as quoted by IRIB. The remark comes after US President Donald Trump, in a post on Truth Social, said that any future damages caused to ships, cargo, or related maritime assets would be paid for using Iranian money held and controlled by the United States. "Please let this statement serve to represent, until further notice, that from this point forth, any and all damages done to Ships, Cargo, or anything related thereto, will be paid for by Iranian Money that the United States has in its possession, and controls," Trump said in his post. He added that the damages "may be very substantial" but described the move as "the fair and equitable thing to do." Iran's Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi criticized Trump's plan to use Iranian assets held by Washington to compensate for damages to ships and cargo transiting through strategic maritime waterways in West Asia, calling the move an "incendiary precedent." In a post on X, Araghchi warned that confiscating another country's assets to settle unrelated claims would undermine international norms and create wider instability. "Seizing another nation's assets to pay for unrelated future claims is an incendiary precedent. Those who celebrate or profit from such funds should remember: once governments normalise confiscation, no one's assets are safe. Ensuing chaos will not be pretty or peaceful," the post read.

news.title: China's singing sailors could be latest weapon in fight for South China Sea
news.text:
A sailor stares mournfully across the ocean, remembering a lover left onshore.

A sleek coast guard ship glides through an endless ocean, passing dolphins and coral reefs.

And a gentle guitar swells to an emotional high, as a singer warbles in a melancholy, smooth falsetto.

This isn't an ordinary love song; it's a declaration of devotion to China.

"Patrolling the South China Sea, guarding every sunrise and moonset over the sea," the singer proclaims.

"Guarding the distant flickering lights of myriad homes, and guarding in my heart little you and the little me."

The song, I Miss You On the South China Sea, was first released by Chinese state media earlier this year, complete with a slick music video showcasing coast guard vessels and personnel.

An English translation version debuted this month, almost exactly 10 years after an international tribunal ruled Beijing's sweeping claims to the hotly contested waterway were not valid.

It might be slightly unconventional, but experts say it's part of a broader propaganda push to reinforce China's claims to the South China Sea — and to humanise the sailors on board the vast flotilla of Chinese Coast Guard vessels that try to enforce it.

Or, in the words of the singer, "Guarding you and me in my heart, and our beloved motherland."

What was the South China Sea arbitration?

Several nations have made various claims to islands and waters within the Western Pacific Ocean for generations, but tensions between China and the Philippines reached boiling point during the 2012 Scarborough Shoal stand-off.

The Philippines took the dispute to the United Nations Convention of Law and the Sea to test China's historic claims to the waters within the so-called "nine-dash line".

The tribunal found China's claims had no legal basis and China had violated the Philippines' sovereign rights, however, China has refused to accept or recognise this ruling.

On the 10th anniversary of the ruling, 14 nations including Australia, the US and the Philippines released a joint statement reaffirming their "unwavering commitment to maintaining a free and open Indo-Pacific that is peaceful, stable, and rules-based, anchored in international law".

"We reaffirm that the Award rendered ten years ago by the Arbitral Tribunal is a significant milestone and is final, legally binding, and definitive between China and the Philippines," the statement said.

The ABC has contacted China's Defence Ministry and Coast Guard for comment, but has not yet received a response.

Complex history missing in action

This fraught and contested history is omitted from I Miss You On the South China Sea, which sticks with picturesque shots of ships at sunset and the romantic musings of the anonymous Chinese sailor at its heart.

Sections of the music video were purportedly filmed on one of Asia's most contested maritime features, the Scarborough Shoal, where Beijing is planning to establish a nature reserve.

The idyllic imagery is a long way from the usual news stories about the Chinese Coast Guard in the South China Sea, which typically hits the international headlines during its episodic confrontations with the Philippines coast guard, like the skirmish last week when personnel allegedly struck each other with oars, sticks and wooden batons.

In contrast, not a soul or vessel from another country features in the music clip, which shows a Chinese Coast Guard vessel in splendid isolation, tracing long arcs through empty waters, disturbed by nothing more threatening than a seagull.

"Guarding endless loneliness, endless vastness, and guarding this sea, this peace and harmony."

There are also a few slightly awkward notes, at least in the English language version.

At one moment the mysterious Chinese sailor sings that his bond with his lover proves the principle of "quantum entanglement", a term used largely by physicists who have suggested that particles of the same origin, and which once were connected, will always stay connected.

Who is the song for?

Graeme Smith, an associate professor at the Australian National University, said the song reflected the regime's "obsession with soft power" and "desire to shape the international narrative".

"It's something that China's been trying to do for a very, very long time and I think they're getting a bit better at it," he said.

But Dr Smith said the "emotional themes" and narrative suggested the song was targeted at a domestic audience and only translated after it had become a hit at home.

"And that's why it feels weird — because we were never the intended audience."

While the video may not top the charts outside of China, the country's reputation is on the rise in parts of the Asia Pacific.

A recent Pew Research Center study found most citizens in Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand, Sri Lanka and Pakistan had a favourable perception of China.

Recent polling from the Lowy Institute also found Australians now trusted China almost as much as the US, largely thanks to a dramatic fall in trust in America following the election of President Donald Trump.

But Dr Smith said China could lose its goodwill if it pursued its agenda too aggressively.

"They need South-East Asian countries to be on board with them," he said.

"Particularly these days with the world order shifting so drastically, they don't want to push so hard that they alienate ASEAN countries and push them towards America."

Not all content is made equal

China, like many nations, has a long history of music, films and literature that help reinforce national pride and priorities.

In times of conflict, lovers separated by duty is a well-worn storyline in both the East and West.

But China has also used music to highlight its technological and economic achievements, such as in 2019 when state news agency Xinhua released a rap ahead of its annual parliament meeting, the two sessions.

But this month, state-run newspaper China Daily was heavily criticised by the Filipino government for releasing an AI-generated video that depicted its countrymen as monkeys.

Manila demanded the "racist" and "offensive, distressing and unacceptable" video be removed.
news.summary: China's state media releases an English version of a love ballad about lovesick sailors in the South China Sea.

news.title: GOP governor survives challenge from Bitcoin evangelist in gubernatorial runoff
news.text: South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden fended off a primary challenge from businessman and Bitcoin evangelist Toby Doeden on Tuesday, winning the first gubernatorial primary runoff in state history and advancing to the November general election. The Associated Press called the race for Rhoden shortly after 9:00 p.m. Eastern. The election marked the first time South Dakota voters were asked to settle a gubernatorial nomination through a primary runoff. State law requires a runoff between the two leading candidates when no contender for governor, U.S. Senate or U.S. House receives at least 35% of the primary vote. TRUMP-BACKED FIREBRAND WINS ARIZONA GOP GOVERNOR PRIMARY, SETTING UP HIGH-STAKES SHOWDOWN The head-to-head contest followed a four-way June primary in which Doeden finished first with 30.6% of the vote and Rhoden placed second with 25.2%, leaving both short of the 35% needed to secure the nomination outright. Rhoden became governor in early 2025 after Kristi Noem left to join the Trump administration, while Doeden entered the race as a businessman and political newcomer. Tuesday’s winner advances to face former Democratic state Sen. Dan Ahlers in November. South Dakota has not had a Democratic governor since Harvey Wollman left office in 1979, and no Democrat has been elected to the office there since Richard Kneip won re-election in 1974. Wollman became governor automatically as lieutenant governor when Kneip resigned. TRUMP FLEXES GOP MUSCLE IN ARIZONA PRIMARIES AS DEMS DODGE FAR-LEFT UPSET In the run-up to Tuesday's primary runoff, property taxes were among the defining issues of the campaign. Doeden campaigned on eliminating property taxes, while Rhoden’s campaign portrayed Doeden’s proposal as fiscally reckless, arguing it could leave local governments and schools with a major funding shortfall. Meanwhile, Rhoden's campaign highlighted other tax relief measures that the governor signed back in March, which Rhoden's campaign website describes as the "largest" property tax cut in the state's history. During the race, Doeden portrayed Rhoden as part of South Dakota’s entrenched political class, declaring after the June primary that "the career politicians told me" an outsider could not break through against three longtime officeholders. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Rhoden pushed back on the attack, saying Doeden was trying to "make hay" out of calling him a career politician and describing that characterization as "such a warped viewpoint," during an interview with the South Dakota Public Broadcasting network. Rhoden argued that his years in the Legislature gave him practical experience writing laws and then returning home to live under them. President Donald Trump did not publicly weigh in with an endorsement in the runoff, according to a review by Fox News Digital. Trump thanked Rhoden by name during his July 3 remarks at Mount Rushmore but did not mention the governor’s race. Doeden, meanwhile, campaigned as a "fierce Trump supporter" who said he would help implement the president’s "America First agenda."
news.summary: South Dakota's first gubernatorial primary runoff pitted incumbent Larry Rhoden against outsider Toby Doeden after neither cleared the 35% threshold to win outright.

news.title: 'Finish this fight': Trump posts video after Iran's surprise attack, talks with Netanyahu
news.text:
The US military said it intercepted multiple ballistic missiles launched by Iran in an attempted surprise attack on American forces in West Asia on Tuesday, bringing an end to a brief lull in hostilities between the two countries. US Central Command (Centcom) said all the incoming missiles were destroyed before reaching their intended targets.
In a statement posted on social media, Centcom said, “At 5:45 p.m. ET today, Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps forces launched multiple ballistic missiles from Iran in an attempted surprise attack on US forces based in the Middle East.”
“All Iranian missiles were successfully intercepted. US forces remain vigilant and at a high state of readiness.”
The attempted strike unfolded just hours after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu held talks with US President Donald Trump at the White House, where the two leaders focused on Iran's nuclear programme and regional security. Both reaffirmed their commitment to preventing Tehran from acquiring nuclear weapons.
Following the meeting, a senior Israeli official said Netanyahu believes Israel has "no choice" but to launch fresh military strikes against Iran, describing his discussions with Trump as "very good and very positive".
The White House meeting came amid growing speculation that Israel and the US were weighing fresh action against Iran before Tehran launched its attempted surprise missile strike.
Attack follows Trump's remarks on Iran
The missile launch came roughly a day after US President Donald Trump said Washington had halted strikes on Iran and claimed Tehran wanted to resume talks.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei appeared to reject that assertion, saying, “We have no negotiations with the United States at present.”
The attempted strike ended a multi-day pause in fighting that had followed nearly two weeks of nightly exchanges between Iran and the US.
Trump shares video Following the missile attack, Trump shared a video on social media with the caption, "Finish this fight." In the video, he is seen walking as a voiceover says, "People have asked me, please, please, please, Mr. President, we're winning too much. We can't take it anymore. We're not used to winning."
Finish this fight. pic.twitter.com/1hRMUbscR6
— The White House (@WhiteHouse) July 28, 2026
Further escalation as Saudi Arabia launches strikes in Iraq
Saudi Arabia said it carried out "limited, targeted strikes" alongside the US on Wednesday against Iran-backed militias in Iraq, saying the groups were linked to attacks on Saudi oil facilities, according to a statement from the Kingdom's Ministry of Defence.
Earlier in the day, the ministry said Saudi air defences had intercepted and destroyed several drones launched from Iraq that were targeting oil facilities in the country's eastern region.
In a separate statement, US Central Command said US and Saudi "fighter aircraft struck multiple terrorist logistics and weapons sites across eastern Iraq" in response to continued drone attacks.
The Saudi defence ministry said the Kingdom "does not seek escalation but will respond to any aggression against it".
An Iranian official denied any involvement in the projectiles fired at targets in Saudi Arabia.
The operation marks the first time Riyadh has publicly acknowledged carrying out strikes inside Iraq since the Iran-US war began.
Although Saudi Arabia has come under repeated attacks from Iran during the conflict, it had largely avoided direct military retaliation until now.

news.text:

news.title: US Senate Delivers Overwhelming 86–12 Bipartisan Backing for Russia Sanctions as Zelensky Watches
news.text:
The US Senate overwhelmingly advanced sweeping sanctions legislation targeting Russia’s energy revenues Tuesday, voting 86–12 to move forward with a bill designed to hit one of the Kremlin’s most important sources of funding for its war against Ukraine.

The decisive bipartisan vote cleared the legislation’s first procedural hurdle and gave new momentum to a sanctions package championed for more than a year by the late Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham.

President Volodymyr Zelensky was in Washington as the vote took place, following talks with President Donald Trump at the White House, Graham’s funeral and a meeting with senators on Capitol Hill.

“Sanctions pressure on Russia is very important,” Zelensky told reporters ahead of the vote, saying the measure would weaken Moscow’s ability to finance its invasion while sending a strong message of support to Ukraine.

“It’s also a big signal to Europe, big signal to Ukraine, big support of our people, so I’m very thankful,” he said.

Targeting the money behind Putin’s war

The legislation goes directly after one of Russia’s greatest remaining advantages: the billions of dollars Moscow continues to earn from energy exports despite years of Western sanctions.

It would impose primary and secondary sanctions on Russian officials, oligarchs and their families, banks and financial institutions, foreign actors supporting Moscow’s war effort and vessels belonging to Russia’s so-called shadow fleet used to bypass restrictions on oil exports.

The bill would also give Trump authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on goods from countries that remain among the largest purchasers of Russian oil and natural gas.

The revised measure focuses those tariffs on the five largest importers of Russian crude oil or gas and the five countries most heavily involved in helping Moscow evade energy sanctions.

That could place major buyers such as China and India under significantly greater pressure to reconsider purchases that continue providing the Kremlin with the money it needs to finance missile production, recruit troops and sustain its war machine.

“This bill is the one that will pass. This bill is the one that the president will sign,” Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal, who developed the legislation alongside Graham, said after the vote.

86–12 sends Moscow a clear message

An 86–12 margin demonstrated that tougher action against Russia retains overwhelming bipartisan support in the Senate despite months of political debate over Ukraine policy.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer framed the vote as a direct warning to the Kremlin.

“With this vote, we are going to show Putin he can’t bully Ukraine,” Schumer said.

For Moscow, the result undercuts hopes that political divisions in Washington could weaken US pressure or allow Russia to simply wait out Western support for Kyiv.

The legislation had spent months stalled despite attracting more than 60 co-sponsors, largely because of negotiations over tariff powers and the White House’s role in implementing them.

Graham announced shortly before his sudden death on July 11 that an agreement with Trump had finally cleared the way for the bill to move forward.

The revised version narrowed an earlier proposal that threatened tariffs of up to 500% against countries buying Russian energy, replacing it with a more targeted framework capped at 100%.

That compromise appears to have unlocked the broad coalition needed to move the legislation through the Senate.

Zelensky takes Ukraine’s case directly to Congress

Before senators entered the chamber, Zelensky met lawmakers behind closed doors and made the case for stronger pressure on Russia, more air-defense support and continued US backing for Ukraine.

All 100 senators had been invited.

The message from Kyiv was straightforward: Russia has not abandoned its war aims, and diplomacy will have little chance of succeeding unless Moscow is confronted with greater military and economic costs.

Earlier in the day, Zelensky met Trump in the Oval Office, where the two discussed licenses allowing Ukraine to produce Patriot interceptors domestically and ways to revive stalled negotiations with Russia.

Zelensky called the talks a “good meeting,” while the White House described them as “positive and productive.”

Taken together, the White House meeting and the Senate vote pointed toward a stronger US approach: improve Ukraine’s defenses, tighten pressure on Russia’s war economy and use that leverage to strengthen Kyiv’s position in any future negotiations.

Graham’s final campaign gains momentum

The bill now bears Graham’s name – the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026.

Graham had been one of Ukraine’s most forceful advocates in Congress and spent his final months arguing that Russia’s ability to wage war depended heavily on foreign buyers continuing to finance Moscow through energy purchases.

Just one day before his death, Graham was in Kyiv meeting Zelensky on what became his 10th visit to Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.

Zelensky traveled to Washington partly to attend Graham’s funeral and described him as “a true friend of Ukraine.”

Six Republican and Democratic senators who reached the final agreement on the sanctions package said there was “no greater way to honor Senator Graham’s legacy” than advancing the measure.

The revised legislation also extends sanctions authority aimed at restricting financing for Iran’s energy and weapons sectors, provisions added at Trump’s request.

Momentum now shifts toward passage

The bill still has additional Senate steps before a final passage vote, but the 86–12 result gives supporters a commanding bipartisan foundation.

The vote also increases pressure on the House of Representatives to take up the measure when lawmakers return to Washington in September.

After months of uncertainty over Washington’s direction, the Senate has now shown that a powerful bipartisan coalition is prepared to impose far greater costs on Moscow and on the countries continuing to bankroll its war.

news.title: South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden fends off GOP challenger in primary runoff
news.text: South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden has won his Republican primary, NBC News projects, after he was forced into a runoff in his bid for a full term in office. He defeated businessman and political newcomer Toby Doeden in a one-on-one matchup Tuesday after no candidate won 35% of the vote in the initial June primary. Rhoden will face off in the November general election against Democrat Dan Ahlers, a former state senator, in the solidly red state. South Dakota has not had a Democratic governor since the 1970s, and the state’s two U.S. senators and lone House member are all Republicans. Rhoden previously served as lieutenant governor and was elevated to the top job in the state after President Donald Trump selected then-Gov. Kristi Noem to serve as homeland security secretary. (She was fired earlier this year.) Now, Rhoden aims to secure his first full term as governor. Doeden had won about 31% of the vote in the June primary, while Rhoden took about 25%. Rep. Dusty Johnson and state House speaker Jon Hansen also sought the GOP nomination for governor, but neither received enough support to advance to the runoff. Rhoden and Doeden both positioned themselves as strong allies of Trump, who did not make an endorsement in the primary. Rhoden framed himself as a candidate with “the proven track record of uniting Republicans from all factions,” while Doeden argued that the state “needs bold conservative leadership, not career politicians.” Rhoden campaigned on cutting property taxes and crime, while touting the state’s lowest unemployment rate in the country. Doeden ran on reducing property taxes, as well as deporting migrants, supporting rural communities and opposing diversity, equity and inclusion efforts in the state. Doeden, poured his own money into his campaign, outspent Rhoden on the airwaves in the runoff. Rhoden also faced attack ads calling him a “career politician” from a super PAC tied to the conservative Club for Growth, although the group has not publicly endorsed in the race.
news.author: Megan Brand

news.title: Oil falls below $84 amid renewed US-Iran diplomacy efforts
news.text:
Global oil prices fell sharply on Tuesday as renewed peace talks between the United States and Iran eased fears of prolonged supply disruptions in the Middle East, with Brent dropping below $84 per barrel after trading above $100 last week.

Data from Oilprice.com showed that Brent, the global oil benchmark, declined from around $87 per barrel on Monday to approximately $83.92 on Tuesday, while the US benchmark, West Texas Intermediate, fell to about $79 per barrel.

The latest decline came as diplomatic efforts between Washington and Tehran gathered momentum, reducing concerns over a prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a critical global oil shipping route through which about a fifth of the world’s crude passes.

Oil prices had surged after the United States launched strikes on Iran on February 28 to stop Tehran from acquiring a nuclear weapon. The ensuing exchange of attacks disrupted shipping in the Gulf and led to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, raising fears of a major supply shock in the global energy market.

The Strait of Hormuz was reopened last month when the US and Iran agreed to a ceasefire. But it was reclosed recently as the two countries exchanged strikes.

However, fresh developments on Tuesday signalled possible progress towards reopening the waterway.

Meanwhile, Reuters reported that Iran had proposed to Oman a temporary arrangement to reopen the Strait of Hormuz under which one direction of maritime traffic would pass through Iranian waters, while part of the opposite route would also transit Iranian territory.

Iran’s Deputy Foreign Minister, Kazem Gharibabadi, told state television that Tehran rejected Oman’s proposal for an equal division of transit routes, arguing that such an arrangement failed to address Iran’s security concerns pending the achievement of long-term regional stability.

He warned that the Strait of Hormuz would remain closed if Muscat rejected Iran’s proposal, adding that Iran had never recognised the southern shipping route along Oman’s coast.

The prospect of renewed oil flows through the strategic waterway helped calm markets, reversing part of last week’s sharp rally.

Similarly, US President Donald Trump said negotiations with Iran were progressing well but warned that Washington was prepared to resume military action if diplomacy failed.

Speaking in an interview with Fox News on Tuesday, Trump said he would prefer to avoid further strikes but threatened to target Iran’s key infrastructure, including power plants, bridges and the underground “Kolang Mountain” nuclear facility, if no agreement was reached.

“I could knock out all their power plants in one day. About 91 million people would be left without electricity and without bridges. But if I can avoid doing that, I’d prefer for it not to happen,” Trump was quoted as saying.

Trump also claimed that most of Iran’s major bridges could be destroyed “in under two hours,” adding that Iranian officials understood the consequences if negotiations broke down.

The US president said Washington would no longer tolerate what it viewed as violations of agreements reached with Tehran, referring to a memorandum earlier signed between both countries.

Ahead of a meeting with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at the White House, Trump dismissed suggestions that he required Israeli intelligence regarding the “Kolang Mountain” facility, insisting that the US already had complete knowledge of the site.

He further claimed that previous American strikes had significantly degraded Iran’s nuclear programme by hitting facilities in Natanz, Fordow and Isfahan during last year’s conflict, warning that the underground facility would also be targeted if negotiations failed.

Global oil prices fall below $84 as renewed US-Iran diplomacy efforts ease fears of supply disruptions and potential Strait of Hormuz reopening.

news.title: Jay Clayton confirmed as US intelligence director
news.text: The Senate has confirmed Jay Clayton to become head of America's intelligence agencies, putting a permanent director in place weeks after President Donald Trump sought to delay his nomination. Clayton, the US lawyer for the Southern District of New York and a former Securities and Exchange Commission chairman, was confirmed 51-47 along party lines. Republicans had initially hoped to confirm Clayton in June, but Trump delayed his hearing in order to allow his temporary pick for the job, Bill Pulte, to take over for several weeks after former director Tulsi Gabbard resigned. Democrats have expressed concerns about Clayton, who lost bipartisan support after a contentious hearing two weeks ago in which he repeatedly refused to say that former US president Joe Biden won the 2020 election. Senator Mark Warner, the top Democrat on the Senate Intelligence Committee, said at the end of the hearing he was "bitterly disappointed" in Clayton. Trump praised Clayton after the vote, writing on social media: "Jay is outstanding in every way, and will do a spectacular job as Director!" The Democratic pushback on Clayton comes as Trump has made revisiting 2020 a primary focus, repeatedly trying to cast doubt on that election and amplifying debunked theories about Biden's win. Clayton said repeatedly at the hearing that the US election was "certified" for Biden, declining to say outright the Democrat won. Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer said he thought Clayton's performance was "abysmal," and that "makes it much less likely that he will get Democratic votes." Clayton emphasised his government and national security experience, attempting to assuage senators in both parties. "I saw firsthand how a strong national security apparatus depends on decisive judgment, discipline, integrity, and effective communication and cooperation across different branches of the government," he said. "If confirmed as Director of National Intelligence, I will commit to upholding these principles every day." Clayton also told senators he had no involvement in Trump's speech about the 2020 election. news.title: US Senate Advances Russia Sanctions Bill, India at Risk of 100% Tariffs
news.text: WASHINGTON: The US Senate advanced sweeping sanctions legislation targeting Russia's energy revenues Tuesday, as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky visited Washington to press for stronger action against Moscow. Senators voted 86-12 to begin consideration of the bipartisan measure, clearing its first procedural hurdle but leaving further debate and a final vote still to come. The bill would impose sanctions on Russian officials, oligarchs, financial institutions and the so-called shadow fleet used to evade restrictions on Moscow's oil exports. It would also give President Donald Trump authority to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on goods from major purchasers of Russian oil and gas, including countries such as China and India. Supporters say choking off energy income is essential to weakening Russian President Vladimir Putin's ability to finance the war in Ukraine, now in its fifth year. The vote came hours after Zelensky met Trump at the White House and attended the Washington funeral of Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, one of Kyiv's most vocal allies in Congress. Zelensky later addressed senators ahead of the vote, seeking support for Ukraine and the sanctions push as fighting intensifies and US-led diplomacy remains stalled. The legislation is named for Graham, who spent more than a year building support for it and reached an agreement with the White House on a revised version shortly before his sudden death earlier this month. "There is no greater way to honor Senator Graham's legacy than to move forward with this bipartisan agreement," six Republican and Democratic senators said in a joint statement. The revised bill also extends existing sanctions authority aimed at restricting funding for Iran's energy and weapons sectors, which was added at Trump's request. Despite broad support for punishing Russia, some Democrats have raised concerns that the tariff provisions hand Trump excessive power and could raise import costs for American consumers or hit European allies. The House has already left Washington for its summer recess and is unlikely to consider the bill before September.

news.title: Iran launches surprise attack on US base
news.text:
The US has said it successfully intercepted a "surprise attack" by Iran on American forces in the Middle East.

Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps forces "launched multiple ballistic missiles in an attempted surprise attack on US forces", US Central Command said on Tuesday evening.

The attacks were reported to have taken place at 5.45 pm ET on Tuesday – the local time in Washington – or around 1.15 am on Wednesday in Iran.

US Central Command did not provide further details about the exact location of the strikes, beyond saying that they were targeting "US forces in the Middle East".

It marks yet another return to conflict, despite Donald Trump saying on Monday that there were "very friendly negotiations going on" during a lull in fighting.

Trump hosted Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli prime minister, in the White House on Tuesday on the five-month anniversary of the war.

It is the first time the pair have met since the US and Israel launched joint attacks on Iran on Feb 28, triggering the conflict in the Middle East.

The Israeli leader described the 90-minute meeting on Tuesday as "one of the best conversations" he has had with Mr Trump, and said the pair discussed "our common goal: ensuring that Iran does not obtain nuclear weapons".

Trump also welcomed Volodymyr Zelensky, the Ukrainian president, for a closed-door meeting in the White House on Tuesday to discuss how Washington might assist Kyiv with missile defence systems.

Karoline Leavitt, Trump's press secretary, said in a post shared later on X that meetings with both foreign leaders were "positive and productive!"

A return to missile strikes in the Middle East will mark a blow for Trump, who has increasingly sought an exit from the conflict before the US midterm elections in November.

Mr Trump had told reporters aboard Air Force One on Monday that "there's a good chance that something could happen" during a period of diplomatic negotiations, while warning that the US would "go back to doing what we were doing" if those talks failed.

Stop-start attacks by both sides over the past few months have repeatedly shattered tentative ceasefire agreements and illustrated the fragility of peace attempts.

Four US soldiers were killed earlier this month during the last ceasefire breakdown.

Three American service members were killed on July 17 when an Iranian missile hit their sleeping barracks at a US base in Jordan, while a fourth soldier was killed in a separate incident in Erbil, Iraq on July 19.

Mr Trump attended a ceremony in Delaware last week honouring the four soldiers after their bodies were returned to American soil in flag-draped caskets.

Credit: X/@sentdefender

Trump has repeatedly promised to obliterate Iran if it does not agree to significant compromises, and renewed that pledge on Tuesday.

"They know I'm going to do that if they don't make a deal," he told Fox News.

"The bridges are going to be gone, literally in less than... I would say in two hours, most of the bridges, the major bridges will all be gone, and the power plants in one day," he said.

Mr Trump also said: "[Iran] cannot have a nuclear weapon. Very simple. And they've agreed to that. Essentially, we have to get them to, you know, make it formal."

The two sides also remain stuck over control of the Strait of Hormuz, the vital waterway through which a fifth of the world's oil supply passed each day before the conflict.

Iran said on Tuesday that it had rejected an Omani proposal to evenly divide control of the Strait between the two countries, which sit either side of the channel.

Tehran said it instead wanted the lion's share of the waterway – something it did not control before the conflict broke out.

The issue has caused the war to spill beyond Iran's borders in recent weeks. Houthi militants in Yemen attacked Saudi Arabian oil tankers in the Red Sea last week, prompting retaliatory strikes from both Riyadh and Yemeni allies.

It pushed oil prices back up to $100 (£75) a barrel last Thursday for the first time since May, extending the global shockwaves of the five-month war.
news.author: Poppy Wood

news.title: US Senate Passes Russia Sanctions Bill — Why India Could Feel the Heat as 100% Tariff Threat Looms
news.text: A proposed US sanctions bill targeting Russia’s energy trade has cleared a key hurdle in the Senate, raising concerns over the possible impact on major buyers of Russian oil, including India. The legislation, which received overwhelming bipartisan support in a 86-12 procedural vote on Tuesday, would give President Donald Trump new powers to impose penalties on countries that buy Russian energy or help Moscow evade sanctions. The bill allows the US President to target the top five buyers of Russian crude oil and natural gas with tariffs, as well as the top five countries accused of assisting Russia’s sanctions evasion, according to the text released on Tuesday. India and China are among the biggest purchasers of Russian energy, meaning they could face economic pressure if the administration decides to use the powers provided under the legislation. The measure has been championed by the late Senator Lindsey Graham and has received backing from Trump, who has indicated support for tougher action against Russia over its war in Ukraine. The bill would allow the President to impose a 500% tariff on Russian goods entering the US and an additional 100% tariff on the top five importers of Russian oil and gas, or countries involved in helping Moscow bypass sanctions. However, the legislation gives the President broad discretion over whether to impose penalties, and it remains unclear how the Trump administration would use the new authority. The vote came after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met Trump at the White House, where he said sanctions pressure on Russia was important. "Sanctions pressure on Russia is very important," Zelenskyy said. "It’s not only about your money. It’s also a big signal to Europe, big signal to Ukraine, big support from all of you. So I’m very thankful." Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer also backed the measure, saying it would send a message to Russian President Vladimir Putin. "With this vote, we are going to show Putin he can’t bully Ukraine, that America stands behind Ukraine," Schumer said. But some lawmakers warned that the legislation could give Trump a wider tool for imposing tariffs. "There is no question that the US government must take stronger action against purchasers of Russian energy who are fueling the unjustifiable war against Ukraine," Senator Ron Wyden and Congressman Richard Neal said. "But the latest draft of the Sanctioning Russia Act is a prescription for bedlam and higher tariffs." The bill would also extend the Iran Sanctions Act of 1996 until 2031, keeping in place penalties on non-US companies doing business with Iran. The bill still needs approval from the House of Representatives, which is currently on its August recess, meaning it cannot become law before September at the earliest. The vote comes after Washington previously imposed tariffs on India over its purchases of Russian energy, before later lifting them as part of wider trade negotiations. China, another major buyer of Russian oil, avoided similar penalties as Trump sought to manage tensions with Beijing. news.title: The U.S. Says It Thwarted An Iranian Missile Attack That Ended A Brief Pause In Fighting
news.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The U.S. military said it knocked down an Iranian ballistic missile attack against American forces in the Middle East on Tuesday, shattering a brief pause in the fighting as mediators tried to get both sides back to negotiations. In addition, American and Saudi forces struck sites used by Iran-backed militias in Iraq to carry out attacks in recent days.

All Iranian missiles were successfully intercepted, the U.S. Central Command said, adding that U.S. forces “remain vigilant and at a high state of readiness.”

The United States and Iran had experienced a period of calm, during which neither announced attacks for days following weeks of escalation over the strategic Strait of Hormuz, the Persian Gulf waterway and narrow chokepoint through which 20% of the world’s oil normally flows.

There was no immediate comment from Tehran on the U.S. military statement or the strikes.

The resumption of fighting comes at the end of a month packed with multiple pressure points on U.S. President Donald Trump over the war. In recent weeks, four U.S. troops died during the fighting, while the Pentagon asked an increasingly skeptical Congress for money to cover the conflict’s ballooning costs.

High gas prices from the continued closure of the Strait of Hormuz are contributing to fears that Republicans are vulnerable in November’s midterm elections. The House narrowly passed a resolution to halt U.S. military action in Iran last week, sending another warning to Trump that reflects the war’s unpopularity with many Americans.

Trump has repeatedly retreated from threats to knock out bridges, power plants and other infrastructure but he told Fox News Channel in an interview earlier Tuesday that Iran knows he’ll “finish the job” if its leaders don’t make a deal to end the war.

Iran had effectively closed the strait when the war began by firing at freighters and tankers off its coast or threatening them. Following the signing of an interim ceasefire deal in June, a battle for control over the strait erupted.

Iran demanded that ships use a route near its coastline and said it can potentially charge fees. Ships were increasingly navigating a southern route along the coast of Oman under a U.S. overwatch operation when Iran attacked some vessels.

Saudi Arabia says it intercepted drone attacks

The U.S. military said Tuesday American and Saudi forces struck sites used by Iran-backed militias in Iraq to carry out attacks in recent days.

“U.S. and Saudi fighter aircraft struck multiple terrorist logistics and weapons sites across eastern Iraq in a strong response to over 30 IRGC-directed aerial drone attacks in the last 72 hours,” U.S. Central Command said in a statement, using an acronym for Iran’s paramilitary Revolutionary Guard.

It said the Revolutionary Guard “and its terrorist proxies must cease these attacks to avoid further U.S. military response.”

The timing of the U.S. military’s separate actions wasn’t immediately clear.

Saudi Arabia said earlier Tuesday that it for a second day shot down drones fired by Iran-backed militias in Iraq, which had attempted to target petroleum facilities in the nation’s eastern region. Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi ordered security agencies to investigate after the Saudis alleged a similar attack on Monday.

Saudi Arabia said earlier on Tuesday that it shot down drones fired by Iran-backed militias in Iraq for a second day, while Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen claimed to have forced a Saudi oil tanker to turn around as part of their self-styled blockade of the kingdom.

The kingdom’s Defense Ministry said in a statement that air defenses intercepted and destroyed several drones that had attempted to target petroleum facilities in the nation’s eastern region. It said the attacks were “once again launched from Iraqi territory and carried out by Iran-affiliated terrorist militias.”

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi ordered security agencies to investigate after the Saudis alleged a similar attack on Monday. The Iraqi military said in a statement that Iraq is committed to “preventing Iraqi territory from being used as a route or launching point for any attack targeting brotherly or friendly countries.”

The Iraqi militias have denied any role in the drone attacks. The Islamic Resistance in Iraq, an umbrella group of Iran-backed armed groups, called the Saudi claims “fabrications” and implied that Monday’s attacks were carried out by the Houthis, who had themselves claimed to have attacked Saudi oil facilities.

A Saudi oil tanker is targeted

Meanwhile, the Houthis claim to have fired missiles at the Saudi oil tanker NCC Ghazal, forcing it to turn back. Last week, they announced a blockade of Saudi shipping, putting another key Middle Eastern waterway — through the Bab el-Mandeb strait leading to the Red Sea — at risk.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Center said a tanker reported hearing explosions while traveling in the southern Red Sea. It did not name the tanker but said the crew and vessel were safe.

The rebels fired on at least one Saudi tanker in the Red Sea last week.

Iran and the U.S. paused their fighting over the weekend, though tensions remain high even as officials said mediators achieved progress in getting the two sides back to negotiations.

Iran said earlier Tuesday that U.S. strikes during an earlier period of escalation destroyed an airport and a marine control tower, and caused damage to 12 bridges and two tunnels, among other infrastructure.

Trump welcomes Netanyahu

Iran’s surprise strikes came as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu visited Washington and Trump. The U.S. and Israel launched the war against Iran on Feb. 28 but Israel has been notably absent from the recent fighting with the Islamic Republic.

Netanyahu said he had an “excellent” meeting with Trump at the White House, their first sit-down since launching the war, which offered Netanyahu a chance to smooth out strains in their relationship.

The closed-door meeting lasted nearly an hour and a half and was “positive and productive,” White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said. The White House did not immediately offer more details.

It comes as both leaders face growing pressures at home. Netanyahu is up for reelection and is embattled in part because of his deteriorating relationship with Trump. Trump is under pressure to end an unpopular war that has wreaked economic havoc and driven prices higher ahead of midterm elections this November.

Concerns over US munitions stockpile

The U.S. ability to intercept Iran’s incoming strikes has become an increasingly salient issue as lawmakers, members of the military and experts raise concerns over the nation’s diminishing stockpiles of missile interceptors.

Sean Parnell, the Pentagon’s chief spokesman, pushed back on those concerns, saying in a statement that the U.S. military “has everything it needs to execute at the time and place of the president’s choosing.”

The Pentagon also said that a new, separate category was created in its official casualty tally for those killed and wounded in the U.S.-Iran fighting because the “Operation Epic Fury” — the military’s official name for combat operations in Iran — had concluded earlier.

The Defense Casualty Analysis System has removed the four soldiers killed and dozens of troops wounded in the latest exchange of fire from its Iran war tally and placed them in a new category called “Overseas Operations.”

Associated Press journalists Konstantin Toropin and Darlene Superville in Washington and Christopher Weber in Los Angeles contributed to this report.

Meanwhile, Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis claimed they fired ballistic missiles at a Saudi oil tanker in the Red Sea for violating their newly declared maritime blockade. Separately, the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency reported that a tanker heard an explosion while transiting the southern Red Sea, though no casualties or damage were reported.Trump warns of more strikes as Iran rules out fresh talksUS President Donald Trump said talks with Iran were progressing but warned Washington was prepared to resume military strikes if diplomacy failed. Iran, however, denied seeking fresh negotiations with the United States and accused Washington of violating last month's framework agreement. The conflict, triggered by US-Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28, continues to fuel instability across the region, with the Strait of Hormuz remaining a key flashpoint.

news.title: Iran and US trade strikes, shattering brief lull in fighting
news.text:
Iran has launched "multiple" ballistic missiles in an "attempted surprise attack" on American forces in the Middle East, the US military said, shattering a lull in the fighting.

The attack occurred at 17:45 EDT (21:45 GMT) on Tuesday, with all missiles "successfully intercepted", said US Central Command (Centcom), which did not disclose any locations of targets.

The US military and Saudi Arabian forces meanwhile struck "Iran-aligned terrorists" in Iraq in retaliation for Iran-directed drone attacks, according to Centcom.

Tehran has not yet commented. The reported crossfire would end a brief break in hostilities between the US and Iran, which was designed to bring negotiators back to the table.

The US and Saudi Arabia struck "multiple terrorist logistics and weapons sites" in eastern Iraq, according to Centcom.

The US military said this was "a strong response to over 30 IRGC-directed aerial drone attacks in the last 72 hours", using an acronym for Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

Centcom said Iran's military "and its terrorist proxies must cease these attacks to avoid further US military response".

Earlier on Tuesday, Saudi Arabia said its military had intercepted and destroyed drones targeting petroleum facilities in the country's eastern region.

Defence ministry spokesman Major General Turki al-Maliki alleged the drones were launched by Iran-affiliated militia groups in Iraqi territory.

The reignited hostilities come a day after US President Donald Trump spoke of "very friendly negotiations" with Iran. At that point, the two sides had not exchanged strikes for a third consecutive day.

Access and control of the Strait of Hormuz remains a key sticking point in talks, which Tehran has denied are even happening.

The latest strikes coincided with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's visit to Washington, where he met Trump at the White House and attended the funeral of US Senator Lindsey Graham, a prominent Iran hawk.

At least 624 US military service members have been wounded since Trump ordered strikes against Iran in February, according to recent Pentagon data.

The Pentagon said 417 of those personnel were injured in relation to Operation Epic Fury, the joint US-Israeli military operation against Iran.
news.summary: US Central Command says it intercepted "multiple" ballistic missiles fired by Iran.

news.title: Ivanka Trump stuns in figure-hugging cut-out gown during chic night out
news.text:
Ivanka Trump showcased her impeccable sense of style as she stepped out in a head-turning cut-out gown over the weekend.

The 44-year-old shared a glimpse of her glamorous evening via Instagram Stories, reposting a photo originally shared by designer Andrea Almeida, in which she posed against a lush tropical backdrop.

The elegant black dress featured dramatic side cut-outs that highlighted Ivanka's toned midriff, while intricate multicolored beadwork through the bodice created a striking focal point. The figure-skimming silhouette flowed into a fringed hem, giving the look a bohemian-inspired finish.

Ivanka wore her signature blonde hair in soft, loose waves and kept her accessories understated, allowing the statement gown to take center stage. She completed the look with oversized earrings and black platform heels.

A fashion-forward moment

Known for her polished, classic wardrobe, Ivanka occasionally embraces more daring silhouettes for special occasions, and this latest ensemble proved to be one of her boldest fashion choices in recent months.

Standing with one hand on her hip amid towering tropical plants, she exuded effortless confidence as she smiled for the camera.

The dress blended intricate craftsmanship with a modern silhouette, making it a standout piece for the evening.

Life in Florida

Ivanka has largely stepped away from politics in recent years, instead focusing on family life with husband Jared Kushner and their three children.

The couple relocated to Florida following Donald Trump's first presidency and now split their time between family commitments, philanthropy and business ventures.

While she maintains a relatively private lifestyle, Ivanka frequently shares snapshots of family vacations, fitness pursuits and elegant fashion moments with her millions of Instagram followers.

Her latest post quickly caught the attention of fans, who praised the sophisticated look and her effortless summer style.

Her appearance comes after Ivanka shared an emotional Father's Day post lamenting Jared's absence from their family getaway at Camp David in Maryland.

"Last Sunday, we gathered at Camp David with my dad, my siblings, our children and their cousins," the 44-year-old began. "Grateful for another Father's Day together."

"Jared couldn't be with us. But his absence was one born on purpose. And we felt his presence all the same," Ivanka continued. "The older I get, the more I realize that family is built in both the extraordinary moments and the ordinary ones: a walk, a laugh, a story shared around the dinner table."
news.summary: Ivanka Trump shared a glamorous new look on Instagram in a striking designer dress. See the photo.
